Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

At @MarketUrbanism , @salimfurth comments on the disappointing fade of the English New Homes Bonus program.

I had never heard of this program until I was working on something else, asked Claude to recommend me some literature, and it recommended me something on the NHB program... and then I was flabbergasted I'd never heard of it.

The NHB at its peak provided English localities with SIX YEARS of property-tax-revenue-equivalents for every new home they permitted. This was thousands of pounds of direct revenue for every home. They spent billions of pounds on this program from 2011-2026 (it has just this year been eliminated).

So, did paying English localities to permit housing work?

Well, I had Claude figure it out. The answer is... maybe slightly?

I instructed Claude to study 4 different ways of analyzing if the program boosted homebuilding. 

First, leveraging a rule change in 2017 that excluded a bunch of localities, we can see if losing the NHB reduced permitting. Answer: no, in fact they maybe increased their permitting after losing the NHB. However, this isn't a clean test: they may have increased their permitting in order to get back into the NHB program by getting over the 0.4% stock additional threshold. So this one is a "Maybe the program kinda worked?" answer.

Second, I was curious about a learning mechanism. You can imagine that pre-NHB, localities that had a "big year" of permitting may have then had "big years" of paperwork, disruptions, and costs, and so "big years" would cause subsequent reductions in permitting. But post-NHB, you can imagine that "big years" of permitting would cause big windfalls of revenues, so might nudge localities to "learn" to permit more. Did Claude find evidence for this? No, not at all. In fact "big years" for permitting seem associated with more NEGATIVE post-year permitting in the post-NHB than the pre-NHB period. Yikes. Talking with @salimfurth he noted that in the post-2017 era, localities might have incentivizes to cluster their permitting all in one year to get over the 0.4% threshold, which could bias these results. Fair.

Third, the NHB was a WAY bigger budgetary impact for some localities (Shire districts) than for others, just because the ratio of new housing construction to municipal budgets varies widely. You'd expect the "more exposed" districts to increase permitting more. The effect here at first seems promising: Shire districts DID have big increases in permits granted! But this is because they had big increases in permits applied for; the actual *rate of granting a permit* DECLINES for Shire districts, despite the NHB literally *paying them to approve*. Moreover, the rise in approvals clearly has a pre-trend before NHB rolled out. NHB also paid localities to clear out long-term empty homes, but we see no Shire-specific reduction in long-term empty homes. So this all suggests little to no effect.

Fourth and finally, the NHB applied *in England only*. We can look at England vs. Wales and Scotland, and then specifically at *municipalities near the borders of England* to see if they changed in a unique way. The answer here is.... maybe? It does look like both the whole regions AND the border-regions only did have higher permitting in England, but it is VERY modest and noisy.

On the whole, this seems like a very big, expensive experiment telling us that "pay for permitting" may not work very well at all. cc @aarmlovi @SCP_Hughes @PeterRFB @johnarnold 

As an aside, this is, I think, a fun case of what Claude allows for researchers. Claude caused my awareness of this program which gets shockingly little attention. I didn't have time to do tons of elaborate analyses myself, so I literally just came up with four possible tests of how the program could be evaluated, and told Claude "here are four ways you could test the program to see if it worked; go do these tests and make sure you use best research practices and very good methods along the way"

Claude didn't do perfectly, and I hope a human housing scholar will go investigate in more detail. But being able to run basically four different quasi-causal models on an intervention *the same afternoon I learned of its existence* and doing so at <1 hour time cost to me, the researcher... y'all, AI is the real deal.

However, as I have said for awhile, I believe $PRME represents a paradigmatic VC-style investment with a long-term upside that dwarfs any other opportunity in biotech history. 

It is far more of a $PLTR or $LLY (or more) in terms of prospective upside, than even an $ALNY or $VRTX or $REGN.

(1) $PRME has the most versatile gene editor, with the demonstrated capability of being able to correct the gene mutations that are the fundamental root cause of monogenic diseases. In fact, it can address 89%+ of the known pathogenic gene variants, if delivery to cells beyond the liver and HSCs can be solved.

(2) Its current primary in-clinic liver targets (AATD, Wilson's Disease) are massive indications in their own right. Success in those alone would justify a valuation north of $10Bn, and we already know that LNPs effectively get gene editors to the liver (see $BEAM).

(4) $PRME has already delivered a functional cure to two patients with the ultra-rare disease Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD).

(5) Importantly, the FDA has now both cleared the way for $PRME to economically develop therapeutics for ultra-rare diseases like CGD by requiring far less clinical data before approval (removing a key drug development bottleneck), as well as cleared the way for far more rapid approval of editors for different mutations that underlie the same genetic disease (again removing a critical drug development bottleneck). This alone is tremendously unique in the biotechnology space.

A library of editors for ultra-rare disease enabled by this regulatory framework is also a substantial source of revenue in its own right.

(6) Finally, David Liu and his lab at the Broad Institute continues to drive substantial innovation in prime editing. The value of a Nobel Prize level scientific talent leading an ongoing innovation engine for a biotechnology company should not be undersold. The value of this work can be seen in things like the OptiPrime AI they developed to optimize the selection of pegRNAs for a given disease.

______

A lot of biotech investors are scared off of a company like this. A few of the reasons include: 

(i) the devastation CRISPR stocks wreaked on portfolios in earlier days
(ii) a lack of precedent for a biotechnology that addresses the known underlying cause of this many diseases with this level of demonstrated efficacy
(iii) the reality that biotech’s graveyard is riddled with promising and much hyped therapeutics that have failed, and an understandable resultant disdain for grand forward looking projections

However, I do think unless a black swan safety event occurs, $PRME holds fundamentally different prospects than other biotechnologies. 

We have simply never had a biotechnology that can fix the underlying cause of this many serious diseases with a swap of an RNA strand, much less have those diseases be ones for which we KNOW precisely what the underlying cause is (in $PRME's case the genetic mutations underlying genetic diseases) AND for which the therapeutic appears capable to the degree of $PRME's editor of actually fixing that underlying cause (in $PRME’s case efficiently writing in new nucleotides in place of genetic mutations in cells it reaches).

The truth is a lot of the classic biotech frameworks don’t really apply here (so long as a platform level safety event doesn't occur, which is its biggest risk, IP protection probably its second), and even the smartest people struggle with context switching and thinking in the exponential. 

In fact, I would say that often times biotech's and pharma's culture biases against these types of grand visions, because they (rightly) understand biology is really, really hard. Far harder than many people in tech seem to appreciate.

At the same time, most generalist investors don’t know enough to understand why $PRME is different than $CRSP,  $EDIT, $NTLA etc.  To them, it’s just another gene editing company, and haven’t those things done terribly? I think therein lies the current opportunity.

A gene editor capable of curing 89% of the genetic variants that underlie genetic disease is precisely that Holy Grail. And, that's even before we start talking about risk factors like APOE4, etc. 

$PRME quite literally ALREADY HAS that editor Anthropic intimated they might someday be able to develop when in full IPO pump mode. 

I have no idea what $PRME’s price does in the short-term. However, I continue to believe it has the potential to transform the face of medicine in unprecedented fashion, and the degree to which it is underpriced is enormous.

Why does Anubis wear the colour of fertile earth?

The black on Anubis’s face carried associations of renewal. Dark Nile silt made crops grow, and black could therefore signify fertility and rebirth in Egyptian religious imagery. That meaning belongs beside his work among the dead: Anubis protected graves and helped prepare bodies for the passage into renewed life. In this painting from Nefertari’s tomb, his dark head meets the queen’s face, still full of warm colour. The colour lets a difficult idea become visible. Death places a person beyond ordinary growth, yet the god attending that passage bears a shade that also promised the land would live again.

Even black could carry the promise of return. If renewal was already hidden in the dark earth, when might an Egyptian have thought a new life actually began?

Image: Anubis and Nefertari, original wall painting in Nefertari’s tomb (QV66), 19th Dynasty. Photo: Onceinawhile / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; square crop, shared under the same licence.

First of all, to break this down fairly, you have to define cheating, and define patterns of behavior

According to a landmark 1992 study led by evolutionary psychologist David Buss at the University of Texas at Austin, men and women process betrayal through entirely different lenses

When surveyed, 60% of men reported that a partner's physical/sexual infidelity was more distressing, whereas 83% of women stated that emotional infidelity was the true dealbreaker

Divorce attorney James Sexton - who I don't always agree with, but does have some valuable insights on the topic of what leads to marital breakdown - perfectly describes this phoenomenon by pointing to reality shows where spouses catch each other cheating, but the question the person being cheated on asks differs depending on their sex. The men ask "Did you fuck him?" While the women ask "Do you love her?"

Men are historically driven by paternity certainty (the fear of raising another man's genetic child), while women are driven by resource and emotional retention (the fear of a partner abandoning the family unit). Equating a transactional, physical encounter with a deep emotional replacement is an intentional misreading of human psychology

The demographic data also completely shatters the idea that women step out at the same rate or in the same way as men do

According to decades of data from the General Social Survey (GSS) analyzed by the Institute for Family Studies, married men consistently cheat at higher rates than married women across almost every age bracket (20% of married men vs. 13% of married women)

He would stop to admire babies in supermarkets, send me pictures of children’s clothes, and tell me how many kids he wanted us to have

When we decided to start trying, I was excited

But month after month, nothing happened

I went to appointments, followed the doctor’s advice, and spent money on tests because I was desperate to understand what was wrong

Kevin always refused to get checked

“Baby, I’m fine. You’re the one who’s worried, so let’s focus on you first”

I should have questioned that, but I loved him

Whenever another month passed, he became distant

Sometimes he would say things like, “Maybe you should have checked your fertility before promising me children”

I would cry in the bathroom so he wouldn’t hear me

My mother told me to stop blaming myself, but I had started believing that Kevin would eventually leave me if I couldn’t give him a child

One evening, after another disappointing appointment, he held me and said, “I love you too much to abandon you over something like this”

I believed him

Two weeks later, a woman sent me a message that began with, “I’m sorry, but you deserve to know who you’re planning to marry”

Attached was a picture of Kevin holding a newborn baby

The caption underneath read, “Daddy’s little girl, six months already”

不知道大家对神经科学了解多少。

我一开始接触神经科学比较晚，大概是2023年的时候。那时在其他人还在感受大一生活的时候，我一心想要创造一个刀剑神域和头号玩家一样的世界，我在知乎发问，跑到国内几乎应该是唯一开设神经科学本科专业的上海纽约大学“求仙问卜”，最后得到的结论是，神经科学，脑科学，电子工程，硬件、软件结合到极致，就算再给人类20年的时间，我也看不到那一天。

当时教授给我的第一个原因是脑。他的理由是人类大脑到今天为止（2023.11我问他的时候），根本没有被彻底建模和理解。这一点不是所谓的脑开发，而是脑机接口做到刀剑神域也就是NerveGear的阶段本质上需要人类科学彻底把脑、意识的问题彻底弄清楚，而如今脑科学领域里，关于大脑的系统论仍然是一盘散沙。

还有就是大众关于侵入式神经科技的认知。侵入式，医疗可用，大众却接受不了芯片入脑（章鱼博士乱入）的不便捷。但如果是非侵入式，解码效率太低，准确性不足。这就是最大的问题之一。

不过，三年过去了，AI发展到今天这个程度，对神经科学、神经科技的发展绝对是有根本性影响的。

现在最大的突破之一，就是连接组学。想想吧，要画出神经元之间的电路图，得在海量电镜切片里追踪每一根神经纤维，以前靠人工几乎不可能完成。AI 自动分割之后，近年来完成了果蝇全脑约 14 万个神经元的连接图，小鼠一立方毫米皮层的图谱也做出来了。
这是在给一盘散沙的系统论补地基。
而且，在各大高校和研究所，用 AI 拟合神经活动，再反过来猜测大脑可能在做什么计算，已经是很活跃的方向。

我可以毫不客气地说，就现在的智能发展速度，脑科学的系统论很有可能不再是一盘散沙。这就好比我们要破解一款超级计算机，以前连电路板上的微米级铜线是怎么连的都不知道，现在AI会直接帮我们把硬件电路图给逆向打印出来。

非侵入式信号效率低、准确性差的问题也可以被AI的高维降噪和模式识别能力暴力破解。
现在的AI，早就不再是死板地去解码某一个特定的脑电波或功能磁共振信号。即使把大脑信号是外星语言。
语义解码器的存在就在于此。
科学家们可以利用类似GPT的架构，让AI去学习人类大脑在思考、听故事、看画面时的脑区激活模式。也就是说，即使非侵入式信号充满了噪音，更强大的AI也能通过强大的上下文预测能力，把这些模糊的信号精准翻译成连续的文本或画面。

神经科学，一定会被AI重塑。我们会通过以脑机接口为主的神经科技看到这一切。
